cards.title: WooCommerce baseline store configuration order
cards.summary: Sequence for standing up a WooCommerce store: deactivate/delete default plugins, set profile, disable comments, install an ecommerce theme with starter site, then configure products, payments, shipping and tax.
cards.use_when: Launching a new WooCommerce store or deciding what to configure first before adding real products and taking live payments.
steps: Deactivate and delete the plugins pre-installed by the host (keeping only the caching plugin, e.g. LiteSpeed Cache) — the source notes leftover plugins can conflict with demo/starter-site imports; they can be reinstalled later.

Set store-owner basics in Users > Profile (color scheme, contact email, password) and disable comments in Settings > Discussion by unchecking comment options and the 'email me whenever' boxes to block spam on a store that does not use blogging.

Install an ecommerce theme (the tutorial uses Bloxy) plus its companion plugin, then import a free starter site using the Elementor builder with a selected set of pages and plugins: theme options, widgets, content, standard plugins and WooCommerce.
Create products: at minimum learn the simple product (single price, no options) and the variable product (size/color combinations) — the source calls these the two most common types.
Connect payments with the Stripe and PayPal WooCommerce plugins, add API credentials, run the connection test, and leave gateways in Test mode until verification succeeds.

Configure shipping as zones (e.g. United States) with flat-rate vs free-shipping minimum thresholds (example: $100) and Shipping Classes such as 'Heavy' to charge per-item rates for oversized products.

Configure tax with the WooCommerce Tax plugin (automatic calculation), the store address, and the origin- vs destination-based method required by the relevant state law; set reduced or zero rates for categories like digital goods.
caveats: Host onboarding screens change frequently; treat the host's exact click path and plan names as of the recording date and verify the current interface.
Free-shipping thresholds and tax methods depend on your jurisdiction and margins — the $100 and US example are illustrations, not benchmarks.
Payment plugins and tax plugins are third-party; confirm current setup steps in their own docs.

cards.title: Simple product configuration in WooCommerce
cards.summary: Field-by-field setup of a WooCommerce simple product, including pricing, sale schedule, inventory rules, shipping dimensions, upsells/cross-sells and category/brand assignment.
cards.use_when: Adding a single-SKU product to a WooCommerce catalog, or auditing an existing product page for missing inventory, shipping or cross-sell data.
steps: Name the product and fill the long description with spec-style content (origin, technicals) that appears below the product; reserve selling copy for the short description, which is the text shoppers see first.
Under Product data choose Simple product; optionally mark Virtual or Downloadable and add files for digital goods.
Set Regular price and Sale price, and use Sale schedule to bound a promotion by date (example in the source: a $100 shirt on sale for $50 from the 6th to the 31st).

Enter the SKU, enable stock management if you want quantities shown on the storefront, set the quantity (example: 10), decide on backorders (example: allow but notify the customer) and set a low-stock threshold (example: 3) so you are alerted before running out.
Add weight and dimensions so shipping rates by weight or size calculate correctly.
Attach an Upsell (shown on this product page, e.g. a matching cap) and a Cross-sell (offered further down the funnel at cart/checkout) — the source distinguishes the two by placement.
Set the main product image and gallery images, assign a product category (creating a new one if needed, e.g. 'Daryl shirts') and add tags or brands.
Publish and view the product page to confirm the price, sale badge, stock count, images, description, additional information and the 'You may also like' upsell block all render.
caveats: Backorder choice is a policy decision: allowing backorders but promising notification means you must fulfil the notification.
The source flags the short description as the most important text because it is what the customer reads first — do not bury key selling points in the long description.

cards.title: Variable product setup for size and color options
cards.summary: How to build a WooCommerce variable product so shoppers can select attributes such as color and size, with per-variation price, stock and image.
cards.use_when: Adding apparel, footwear or any product sold in multiple sizes, colors or materials, or when shoppers cannot currently select a variant on the PDP.
steps: Create the product as normal, then under Product data select Variable product instead of Simple.
Define attributes (e.g. Color, Size) and the values for each attribute; the source demonstrates this style of selection against a real store selling multiple colors and sizes.
Generate variations from those attributes and edit each one individually.
Set stock level, price and (where the option is offered) a variant-specific image for every combination, e.g. Size 10 / Red.
Enforce the rule that a price must be set for each variation — otherwise that combination is not purchasable and the shopper hits a dead option.
Preview the product page and click through each attribute combination to confirm prices, stock and images update as expected.
caveats: Variation count multiplies quickly; every attribute combination is a row to price and stock, so keep attribute lists to what you actually sell.
The source notes attributes only apply to variable products, so do not populate them on simple products.

cards.title: Upsell vs cross-sell placement in WooCommerce
cards.summary: Distinguish WooCommerce upsells (on the current product page) from cross-sells (offered at cart/checkout) and pick which products to place where.
cards.use_when: Merchandising a product page or cart to raise average order value with complementary items.
steps: Treat an Upsell as a recommendation shown while the shopper is viewing the current product — it appears at the bottom of that product page in a 'You may also like' style block.
Treat a Cross-sell as a recommendation shown at checkout/cart after the item is added — used to attach lower-priced or complementary items to an existing basket.
Populate both fields from the product edit screen when creating the product; the source demonstrates an upsell with a snapback cap on a t-shirt product.

Choose the relationship deliberately: on the PDP, offer a comparable or upgraded item (the source's example pairs the shirt with a cap); at cart/checkout, offer additions that complement what is already in the basket.
Verify on the live product page and cart that the correct products surface in each slot.
caveats: The source illustrates the mechanism but gives no AOV results; treat uplift from upsells/cross-sells as something to test on your own catalog rather than an assumed gain.
Adding too many recommendations can clutter the PDP or checkout — the source shows a single slot in each location.

cards.title: Elementor container and flexbox layout for ecommerce pages
cards.summary: Using Elementor containers with flexbox direction, justify-content and per-column width to build clean product and landing layouts that adapt across devices.
cards.use_when: Building or fixing a homepage, category or landing page layout in Elementor — e.g. getting two buttons to sit side by side or making an image column narrower than a text column.
steps: Add a container (click plus) and choose Flexbox rather than Grid — the source calls flexbox easier and the common choice.

Drag elements into the container; note that plain elements such as two buttons stack vertically with no control, so wrap side-by-side items (e.g. 'Shop now' + 'Contact us') inside their own container.
On the container, switch the flex Direction to Horizontal to place children side by side, or Vertical to stack them; use reversed direction to swap order.
Use Justify content to position children — center, start, end, space-between, space-around, space-evenly — rather than adding manual padding.
Adjust per-column Width when one column should be smaller (e.g. an image column narrower than the text column).
For a full-height hero, set the container's Minimum height to 100VH on the section rather than the inner container — the interface itself labels this as the way to achieve full-height containers.
Editing each element exposes three tabs: Content (the text/media itself), Style (typography, colors, sizes) and Advanced (padding/margins and motion effects such as entrance animations).

Use the responsive breakpoints (desktop, tablet portrait, mobile portrait) to re-apply flex settings per device — centering, changing a background image, resizing type or hiding elements only on that device.
caveats: Do not put too many items horizontal in a narrow box: the source shows elements render badly when there is not enough space and recommends vertical plus centered instead.
The source opinion that Gutenberg 'is terrible' and Elementor is the number-one builder is a presenter preference; if you already have a working builder stack, changing it is optional.
Elementor has released 'Atomic Elements' aimed at developers; the tutorial recommends deactivating them while building a store and notes the interface may change.

cards.title: Starter-site import and why to remove conflicting plugins
cards.summary: Importing an ecommerce starter template (theme options, widgets, content and plugins) to get a functioning store skeleton fast, and cleaning up pre-installed plugins first to avoid broken imports.
cards.use_when: Setting up a new store quickly and needing a working shop layout — header, hero, category blocks, product grid — before replacing demo content with real products.
steps: In the theme's dashboard, open Starter Sites, filter to Free plans and select the Elementor builder.
Pick a template and click Import; choose Elementor when prompted for a page builder.
Keep the import options for theme options, widgets and content selected, and confirm it is a clean install so the demo imports without leftovers.
Keep the plugin list selected on the next step — typically the page builder, a contact-form plugin and WooCommerce (the shopping-cart integration) — then click install and wait roughly a minute.

After import, view the site: the starter provides a menu, hero landing section, trust badges (free delivery, 30-day returns, secure payment), dummy products, category blocks (jackets, sweaters, accessories), a popular-products section and a shop page with a filterable sidebar gallery.
Delete or trash demo products afterwards (Products > select all > bulk actions > Move to trash, recoverable from Trash) and replace images and copy with your own.
Import demo pages (shop, services, about us) and adapt them rather than building every page from scratch.
caveats: Delete pre-installed host plugins before importing — the source says they can conflict with the demo import.
The imported content is demo data: replace dummy products, images and text before launch so the storefront is not visibly a template.
Starter-site availability and the import wizard change over time; verify the current flow in your theme.

cards.title: Header settings that block page building and product imagery
cards.summary: Two theme-customizer header toggles — sticky header and transparent header — that interfere with page building and hero images, and when to switch them off.
cards.use_when: Troubleshooting an Elementor editing experience where the menu collides with the builder, or a hero image pushing up under the menu and hiding content.
steps: Open the theme customizer (Websites > Customize) and go to Header > Global Header.
Turn off the sticky-header option if the fixed menu blocks or collides with the builder while you are working — the source disables it purely to remove that friction during building.
Turn off transparent header if the starter template uses one: a transparent header forces page content up under the menu, cuts access to those areas and can push hero imagery into the navigation.
After changing header settings, publish and refresh the Elementor editor to confirm the page now starts below the header and you have space to add sections.
Re-enable sticky header after the build if you want the persistent navigation for shoppers — the source's reason for disabling it was editorial convenience, not a storefront recommendation.

While a hero is being styled, remove any custom position on the background first and set display size to Cover, then pick a focal position (center right vs center center etc.) so subjects are not cropped out.
caveats: These are theme-specific settings; the exact labels live under the theme customizer and may differ by theme.
Disabling sticky or transparent headers changes shopper-facing navigation behavior — decide the final setting on user experience, not just build convenience.

cards.title: Responsive optimization pass across desktop, tablet and mobile
cards.summary: Per-device layout review in Elementor: centering flex content, swapping background images, applying overlays for text contrast, resizing text and hiding elements that break small screens.
cards.use_when: Doing the mobile/tablet pass on a store homepage, category page or landing page before launch, or fixing text that is illegible over an image on small screens.
steps: Switch the editor to each device view (desktop, tablet portrait, mobile portrait) — settings changed while a device view is active are saved scoped to that device.
Center stacked content per device: select the flexbox container and set justify-content to center for tablet and mobile instead of leaving left-aligned rows.
Change background images per device where the desktop crop does not work on mobile — Elementor stores a separate image for the tablet or mobile breakpoint.
Add a background overlay with a darker color and increased opacity when light imagery makes overlaid text unreadable, and scope the overlay to the device that needs it.
Adjust typography size per device for text that reads too small or too large (e.g. enlarge a heading only on tablet portrait).
Hide elements that do not fit small screens: open the element's Advanced settings, find Responsive, and hide it on tablet/mobile — the same controls work for sections and columns.
Re-check the default auto-generated sections; the source notes WooCommerce product displays are automatically responsive, but manual sections and footers still need review.
caveats: Changing a background per device makes maintenance heavier — keep one image across devices unless the desktop crop genuinely fails.
Hiding elements removes information for that audience; check the hidden element is not a required CTA or price.

cards.title: Elementor element editing, copy-paste style and AI page drafts
cards.summary: Working efficiently inside Elementor: the content/style/advanced tab model, duplicating elements and columns, copying style between same-type elements, and using Elementor AI to draft a page quickly.
cards.use_when: Building a reusable store page (About, Team, landing section) and needing to keep typography, colors and spacing consistent without restyling each element by hand.
steps: Select any element to get three tabs: Content for the text, image or link; Style for typography, colors and size; Advanced for padding/margins and motion effects such as entrance animations.
Right-click an element or container to Duplicate or Delete; duplicating a container clones a whole column so you can build repeated card rows quickly.
Configure one element fully, then right-click it and Copy, and on each matching element use Paste style — the source notes this works between the same element type and keeps a page consistent.
For the button link field, type the page name and the builder resolves the page URL automatically, so 'shop now' can be pointed at the Shop page without copying a URL.
For a quick page draft, use Elementor AI: prompt it for a layout (e.g. a three-column row) and click Use layouts, then clean up the result.
Treat AI-generated pages as a starting point: the source's own test requested three columns and got four, so delete extra sections and replace placeholder images and names before publishing.
caveats: The source explicitly rates Elementor's AI builder as 'not the best' but occasionally useful — do not ship its output unchecked.
The demo used a specific font choice (Poppins bold) as a personal preference, not a conversion recommendation; pick one brand font family and apply it consistently.

cards.title: Creating pages, menus and dropdown navigation for a store
cards.summary: Adding WooCommerce pages such as About/Team, assigning them to the site menu, building dropdown submenus and adding external custom links (e.g. a community URL).
cards.use_when: Building out an online store's site structure — adding an Our Team or Services page, organizing the navigation under shop and contact, or linking to an off-site channel.
steps: In Pages > Add Page, create the new page, publish it, then open the Elementor builder to design it (the source drafts a Team page with a three-column layout of images, names and roles).
Go to Appearance > Menus — the menu created at import holds the starter item structure.
Under Pages click View all, tick the new page (e.g. Our Team) and click Add to menu.
Drag the item to the desired position; nest it under a parent (e.g. under Services) to create a dropdown that appears on hover.

To link off-site destinations (a Facebook group or school), use the Custom Links section: paste the URL, give it a label, click Add to menu, then position it (e.g. under a Contact item) and click Save menu.
Visit the live site to confirm the dropdown opens on hover and the custom link resolves to the right destination.
caveats: Menu structure is theme-driven; the dropdown behavior and depth limits come from the theme.
Custom links point off-site, so they take shoppers away from checkout — place them where abandonment risk is low.

cards.title: WooCommerce admin surfaces for running the store after launch
cards.summary: Which WooCommerce admin screens exist and what each one answers for a store operator: orders, customers, coupons, reports and the upgraded analytics view.
cards.use_when: Setting up the operational side of a WooCommerce store — reviewing orders, tracking customers, issuing coupons and checking sales reporting after launch.
steps: Use Orders to review everything customers have purchased; each order appears here as it is placed.
Use Customers to see everyone who has purchased, with username and email, so you can identify repeat buyers or export a list for retention work.
Use Coupons to create and manage discount codes applied on the storefront.
Use Reports for the legacy sales report listing.
Use WooCommerce Analytics for the upgraded view showing total sales, net sales, orders, products sold and related metrics — the source treats this as the primary reporting surface.
Use Settings as the central configuration screen for the store (the source flags it as the most important section, covering the store-level configuration used for payments, shipping and tax).
caveats: The source admits to skipping many WooCommerce options as unnecessary for a basic store; the depth you configure should match your sales volume and tax/shipping complexity.
Metric definitions in Reports vs Analytics differ (total vs net sales) — confirm which figure you are quoting before acting on it.
